query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the selective oxidation or reduction of Al and Ti at grain boundaries and phase interfaces, leading to the formation of brittle intergranular oxides or reduced phases that promote crack initiation and propagation. Catastrophic failure occurs when these embrittled regions coalesce, causing rapid loss of mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a predominantly fcc matrix, as-built microstructure.
generation.intervention: Controlled variation of Al and Ti content (e.g., reduce Al and Ti by 50%) in the alloy composition, while keeping other elements constant.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 800°C) in oxidizing (air) and reducing (hydrogen) atmospheres for up to 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and phase interfaces enriched in Al and Ti, which act as sites for preferential oxidation or reduction.
generation.mechanism: Al and Ti are more reactive than Co, Cr, Fe, or Ni; at high temperatures, they preferentially oxidize (in air) or reduce (in hydrogen), forming brittle oxides or reduced phases at grain boundaries. These phases embrittle the microstructure, facilitating crack initiation and propagation under stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reducing Al and Ti content will decrease the formation of brittle intergranular oxides or reduced phases, resulting in improved resistance to catastrophic failure (i.e., higher time-to-failure and less severe embrittlement) compared to the baseline alloy. The baseline alloy will show rapid crack propagation and catastrophic failure after exposure, while the modified alloy will retain more ductility and structural integrity.
generation.baseline: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exposed to elevated temperature in oxidizing/reducing gases, showing rapid degradation and catastrophic failure.
generation.boundary: Applicable for exposures above 600°C and up to 100 hours; outside this range, diffusion and reaction kinetics may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Lack of direct evidence for the exact microstructural evolution in this specific alloy system under these conditions; uncertainty in the quantitative effect size of Al/Ti reduction.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: baseline alloy and alloy with 50% reduced Al/Ti content. Expose both sets to 800°C in air and hydrogen for 100 hours. Perform microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM), measure mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility), and assess crack propagation.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of grain boundaries and phase interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing Al/Ti content does not significantly decrease the formation of brittle intergranular phases or does not improve resistance to catastrophic failure (i.e., time-to-failure and ductility remain similar to baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.
